checks.topic: Week 5 differentiation treated conceptually: what the derivative is, and why. Covers the first-principles definition f'(x) = lim(h to 0) [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h and why h must approach zero without reaching it; the geometric picture of the tangent as the limiting position of a chord; why each rule takes the form it does (product rule as two separate contributions to the change in a product, quotient rule as a consequence of writing u/v as u times v to the power minus one, chain rule as composition of rates); what higher-order derivatives measure; why implicit differentiation produces a dy/dx factor while partial differentiation does not; and what fails when a function has a corner. No computation is asked for beyond checking a claim.

questions.q: In f'(a) = lim(h to 0) [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h, why must h be allowed to approach 0 but never actually be set equal to 0?
options: Because substituting h = 0 gives 0/0, which has no value; the limit names the number the quotient approaches without ever attaining it
Because substituting h = 0 would make f(a+h) undefined for most functions of interest
Because h must remain strictly positive, since a negative h would measure the chord on the wrong side of the point
Because h = 0 is in fact permitted, and the limit notation is a historical convention retained for tidiness
questions.concept: Why the derivative is a limit and not an evaluation: the difference quotient is undefined exactly at the point of interest.
questions.why: For h = 0 both numerator and denominator vanish, so the quotient is meaningless there. The limit is the whole point of the definition: it extracts the value the quotient tends to on approach.

questions.q: Before the limit is taken, what does the quantity [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h represent on the graph of y = f(x)?
options: The gradient of the tangent to the curve at x = a
The gradient of the chord joining the points (a, f(a)) and (a+h, f(a+h))
The average of the tangent gradients at x = a and at x = a+h
The vertical gap between the curve and its tangent line at x = a
questions.concept: Geometric representation of the derivative: chord gradient before the limit, tangent gradient after it.
questions.why: It is rise over run between two points actually on the curve, which is by definition the gradient of the chord through them; the tangent appears only in the limit h to 0.

questions.q: Why does the derivative of a product uv contain two terms, u'v + uv', rather than a single term?
options: Because differentiation is applied to each factor in turn and the two results are then added
Because u and v each have their own tangent line, and the tangent to the product is the sum of those two tangents
Because over a small increment the product changes by (change in u) times v plus u times (change in v), the product of the two changes being negligible in the limit
Because the product rule is simply the chain rule applied once to u and once to v
questions.concept: The product rule as an accounting of how a product responds when both factors move: two first-order contributions plus a second-order term that dies in the limit.
questions.why: Expanding (u+du)(v+dv) - uv gives du.v + u.dv + du.dv; dividing by h and letting h to 0 kills the du.dv term and leaves exactly u'v + uv'.

questions.q: In dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx), why are the two rates multiplied rather than added?
options: Because du cancels in the fraction (dy/du)(du/dx), and cancellation is only valid for products
Because addition would give the wrong physical units, whereas multiplication keeps the result dimensionless
Because the outer function must be evaluated at u rather than at x, and multiplication is the only operation that respects that substitution
Because rates of change compose: if u changes k times as fast as x, and y changes m times as fast as u, then y changes mk times as fast as x
questions.concept: The chain rule as composition of rates, not as symbolic cancellation of differentials.
questions.why: Sensitivity is multiplicative under composition: scaling one link by k and the next by m scales the whole chain by mk. The du-cancels picture is a mnemonic, not a reason, since dy/du is a limit rather than a genuine ratio of numbers.

questions.q: Why is the numerator of the quotient rule u'v - uv' rather than uv' - u'v?
options: Because the numerator has to come out positive whenever the quotient is an increasing function
Because the derivative of a denominator carries a minus sign in every rule of differentiation
Because u/v = u times v to the power -1, and the product plus chain rules give u'v^-1 - uv^-2 v', which over the common denominator v squared is (u'v - uv')/v squared
Because the order is only a convention; either arrangement is acceptable provided it is used consistently
questions.concept: The quotient rule is derived, not memorised: rewriting as a product with a negative index fixes both the order of the terms and the v squared denominator.
questions.why: Differentiating u.v^-1 by the product rule gives u'v^-1 + u(-v^-2)v'; putting that over v squared produces u'v - uv' in that order. Swapping the terms changes the sign of the answer and is genuinely wrong, not a variant convention.

questions.q: Why does f(x) = |x| have no derivative at x = 0?
options: Because |x| is not continuous at x = 0
Because the difference quotient tends to -1 as h approaches 0 from the left and to +1 from the right, so no single limit exists
Because the gradient at x = 0 is infinite, as it is at a vertical tangent
Because |x| is defined piecewise, and a piecewise function is never differentiable where the pieces meet
questions.concept: Differentiability requires the two one-sided limits of the difference quotient to agree; continuity alone is not enough.
questions.why: For h < 0 the quotient |h|/h equals -1 and for h > 0 it equals +1, so the limit fails to exist. The function is perfectly continuous there and its gradient is bounded, so neither discontinuity nor an infinite slope is the reason.

questions.q: What does the second derivative f''(x) measure?
options: The rate at which the gradient of the curve is itself changing
The square of the first derivative, since differentiating twice multiplies the rate by itself
The gradient of the tangent line drawn to the tangent line
The total change in the function across two successive intervals of x
questions.concept: Higher-order derivatives: f'' is the derivative of f', describing how the slope evolves (concavity, acceleration).
questions.why: f'' is defined as d/dx of dy/dx, so it reports how fast the slope is changing. It is not the square of f' (for y = x cubed, f'' = 6x while (f')squared = 9x^4), and the tangent line is straight so its own gradient is constant.

questions.q: When x squared plus y squared = 25 is differentiated with respect to x, why does the y squared term give 2y(dy/dx) rather than just 2y?
options: Because dy/dx is a constant of differentiation that appears whenever two variables occur in one equation
Because the equation has not been solved for y, so a factor dy/dx is inserted to keep the two sides balanced
Because y is squared, and the chain rule contributes one extra factor for every power above the first
Because y stands for a function of x, so d(y squared)/dx = d(y squared)/dy times dy/dx = 2y times dy/dx
questions.concept: Implicit differentiation is the chain rule: differentiating an expression in y with respect to x costs a factor dy/dx because y depends on x.
questions.why: The differentiation variable is x but the expression is written in y, so the chain rule inserts dy/dx. The factor is not a balancing device and does not depend on the size of the power; it appears for any function of y, including y itself.

questions.q: Explain why the gradient of the tangent at a point must be defined as a limit of chord gradients, rather than computed directly from the single point at which the tangent touches the curve.
questions.concept: Why the derivative needs a limit at all: gradient is a two-point notion, but the tangent touches at only one point.
questions.why: A full answer states that gradient is defined as rise over run between two distinct points, so a single point gives 0/0 and no gradient. The only way to speak of the slope at one point is to take a second point on the curve a distance h away, compute the chord gradient [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h, and see what value that gradient approaches as the second point slides towards the first. The chord rotates towards a limiting line; that limiting line is the tangent and its gradient is f'(a). It should also note that the limit may fail to exist (corner, or disagreeing one-sided limits), in which case there is no tangent and no derivative.

questions.q: Explain why d/dx[c f(x)] = c f'(x) is valid while d/dx[f(x)g(x)] = f'(x)g'(x) is not, in terms of what happens to the difference quotient in each case.
questions.concept: Linearity of differentiation versus the failure of multiplicativity: what a constant does inside the difference quotient versus what a second varying factor does.
questions.why: A full answer works with the quotient. For cf, [cf(x+h) - cf(x)]/h = c[f(x+h) - f(x)]/h, so the constant factors straight out of the limit and reappears untouched: c does not change as x changes, so it contributes nothing of its own. For a product, [f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)]/h does not separate that way; adding and subtracting f(x)g(x+h) splits it into g(x+h)[f(x+h) - f(x)]/h + f(x)[g(x+h) - g(x)]/h, which tends to f'g + fg'. The point is that both factors move, so the change in the product picks up a contribution from each, and f'g' captures neither. A concrete counterexample such as y = x cubed times (2x+5), where f'g' = 6x squared but the true derivative is 8x cubed + 15x squared, completes the answer.

questions.q: Explain why, in computing the partial derivative of f(x, y) with respect to x, the variable y is held constant, and why no dy/dx factor appears even though the function contains y.
questions.concept: Partial versus implicit differentiation: whether y is an independent variable or a function of x.
questions.why: A full answer says that in f(x, y) the two variables are independent inputs, so the partial derivative asks a one-directional question: how does the output respond when x alone is nudged and y is pinned. Since y is not changing, every expression in y is a constant for that computation and contributes no rate of its own, so no dy/dx term can arise. Geometrically, the surface z = f(x, y) is sliced by the plane y = constant and the ordinary derivative of the resulting curve is taken. It should contrast this with implicit differentiation, where the equation constrains y to be a function of x, so nudging x forces y to move and the chain rule inserts dy/dx.

questions.q: Explain why, for a curve given parametrically by x = x(t) and y = y(t), the gradient is dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and explain what goes wrong at a value of t where dx/dt = 0.
questions.concept: Parametric differentiation as a chain-rule consequence, and the geometric meaning of dx/dt = 0.
questions.why: A full answer derives it from the chain rule: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt), so provided dx/dt is not zero one may divide to get dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). It should say why dy/dt alone is not the gradient: it measures how fast y changes with the parameter, which depends on how quickly the curve is traced, whereas the gradient of the curve is a purely geometric quantity independent of the parametrisation. Where dx/dt = 0 the point is momentarily not moving horizontally, so the division is invalid; the tangent there is vertical (if dy/dt is non-zero) and dy/dx is undefined, or the point may be a cusp if dy/dt vanishes too.

checks.topic: Conceptual hour on Week 5 circuit analysis. What Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule each assert, and which conservation principle each one expresses: charge conservation with no accumulation at a node in the steady state, and conservation of energy per unit charge expressed as the single-valuedness of electric potential. Why the traversal sign rules take the form they do, in particular why the sign of an IR term depends on the direction of travel relative to the assumed current while the sign of an emf term depends only on the order in which the terminals are crossed. What goes wrong without a consistent convention, why only n minus 1 junction equations are independent for n junctions, and why a bridge circuit falls outside the series and parallel combination rules.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule states that the algebraic sum of the currents at a junction is zero. What physical principle is that a statement of?
options: Energy is conserved, so the charges arriving at the junction carry the same energy as those leaving it.
Every point of a junction sits at the same potential, and that equality forces the currents to be equal.
Charge is conserved and cannot accumulate at a point in the steady state, so it arrives and leaves at equal rates.
Current always divides at a junction so as to follow the path of lowest resistance available to it.
questions.concept: The junction rule as charge conservation under the steady-state condition of no charge accumulation
questions.why: The rule counts charge per second in and out. Charge is conserved, and in a steady current there is no build-up of charge at a point, so the two rates must be equal. It says nothing about energy or about potentials being equal.

questions.q: The loop rule says the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero. What makes that true?
options: Electric potential is single-valued, so a charge taken once round a closed path returns to the potential it started at.
The current is the same at every point of a closed loop, so the potential changes across the elements must cancel.
A battery supplies exactly as much charge as the resistors consume, so the loop balances over one full circuit.
The total resistance measured around any closed conducting loop necessarily comes out to be zero.
questions.concept: The loop rule as conservation of energy per unit charge, i.e. potential is a single-valued function of position
questions.why: Potential is a function of position, so returning to the same point returns you to the same value; the energy a unit charge gains from sources round the loop equals what it loses in resistances.

questions.q: While walking a loop you pass through a resistor R in the same direction as the assumed current I. Why is the term entered minus IR rather than plus IR?
options: Because charge is used up inside the resistor, so less charge leaves it than entered it.
Because a resistor opposes the flow of current, and any opposing element is entered with a negative sign.
Because the loop happens to be walked clockwise, and clockwise traversals are conventionally negative.
Because current inside a resistor runs from high to low potential, so moving with it is moving downhill.
questions.concept: Why the resistor sign follows from the direction of potential drop relative to the direction of travel
questions.why: In a resistor the current flows from the higher-potential end to the lower-potential end. Travelling in that same direction is travelling to a lower potential, so the potential change is negative.

questions.q: What fixes the sign of an emf term when you write a loop equation?
options: Whether the assumed current leaves the source at its positive terminal or enters the source there.
The order in which the traversal crosses the terminals: minus to plus gives plus epsilon, plus to minus gives minus epsilon.
Whether the source is delivering energy to the circuit or is absorbing energy from the rest of the circuit.
Whether the loop as a whole is being traversed clockwise or anticlockwise around the circuit diagram.
questions.concept: The emf sign is set by terminal order alone, independently of current direction and of charging or discharging
questions.why: An emf term is the potential difference between the source's terminals, which is fixed by which terminal you enter and which you leave. The current direction is already accounted for separately in the Ir term.

questions.q: A student solves a two-loop network and one branch current comes out negative. What does that tell them about the work they have done?
options: Nothing is wrong: the magnitude is right and the real current runs opposite to the arrow that was drawn.
One of the loop equations carries a sign error, because a real steady current cannot have a negative value.
The current arrows must all be redrawn the correct way round and the whole system solved again from scratch.
That branch is discharging, so its current is falling with time and the number found is only an instantaneous value.
questions.concept: The assumed current arrows are a sign convention, not a physical claim; the algebra reports a reversed guess as a minus sign
questions.why: The equations are linear in the currents and are written consistently with whatever arrows were chosen, so a reversed guess simply returns the same magnitude with the opposite sign.

questions.q: A network has 4 junctions and 6 branches. How many independent junction equations can be written for it?
options: Four, because each junction imposes its own constraint on the currents meeting there.
Six, because one equation is needed for each of the branch currents that must be found.
Three, because the fourth is the sum of the other three and carries no new information.
Two, because one junction equation belongs to each independent loop that can be drawn.
questions.concept: Redundancy among junction equations: for n junctions only n minus 1 are independent
questions.why: Adding all the junction equations together gives zero identically, since every branch current enters one and leaves another, so any one of them can be derived from the rest.

questions.q: Why can an unbalanced bridge circuit not be reduced to one resistance using only the series and parallel rules?
options: Because it contains more than one source of emf, and the combination rules assume there is only one.
Because no two of its resistors carry the same current or span the same pair of nodes.
Because its resistances are unequal, and the parallel formula only holds for equal resistances.
Because the current in the bridge arm keeps reversing, so it has no steady value that can be combined.
questions.concept: The conditions that define series (same current) and parallel (same pair of nodes), and why a bridge satisfies neither
questions.why: Series requires that the same current be forced through both elements and parallel requires that both ends be common; the bridge arm breaks both conditions for every pair in the network.

questions.q: Exactly two conductors meet at point c in a circuit diagram. Why is c not a junction for the purposes of the current rule?
options: Because c lies in the interior of a loop rather than on the boundary between two adjacent loops.
Because the potential at c is zero, so no meaningful current equation can be written at that point.
Because no current passes through c at all, the connection there being nothing more than a joint.
Because only two conductors meet, so the same current passes on and there is nothing to divide.
questions.concept: Definition of a junction as a point where three or more conductors meet, and why two-conductor points give no new equation
questions.why: With only two conductors the current entering must equal the current leaving trivially; the equation is the identity I equals I and contributes nothing to the solution.

questions.q: Explain why the loop rule can legitimately be applied to a network before you know the actual directions of any of the currents.
questions.concept: Assumed current directions function as sign definitions; both Kirchhoff rules are linear in the currents
questions.why: A full answer says that drawing an arrow defines what counts as positive current in that branch rather than asserting a fact about the circuit; that every loop and junction equation is then written consistently with those definitions; that because both rules are linear in the currents, a definition chosen opposite to reality yields the same solution with that current's sign reversed; and therefore the physics enters only through the emfs, resistances and topology, never through the guess.

questions.q: Explain why the sign of a resistor term in a loop equation depends on the direction you traverse the loop, while the sign of an emf term does not depend on the direction of the current in that branch.
questions.concept: The two sign rules have different origins: IR is a potential change produced by the current, epsilon is a fixed property of the source's terminals
questions.why: A full answer says the loop equation sums potential changes along a chosen path, so every term's sign is set by which end you enter and which you leave. For a resistor the high-potential end is determined by the current direction, so the sign depends on travel direction relative to the current arrow. For a source the plus and minus terminals are fixed by its construction, so the sign depends only on terminal order; whether the source is charging or discharging is carried entirely by the separate Ir term and by the sign of the solved current, not by the emf term.

questions.q: Explain why the junction rule would fail if charge were allowed to accumulate at a junction, and why the steady-state assumption is what rescues it.
questions.concept: The junction rule is charge conservation plus the steady-state condition dQ/dt equals zero at a node
questions.why: A full answer says charge conservation alone gives current in minus current out equals the rate of increase of charge stored at the node. If charge accumulated, that rate would be non-zero and the sum of currents would not vanish, as happens at a capacitor plate while it charges. In a steady current nothing at a junction changes with time, so the stored charge is constant, the rate is zero and the currents balance exactly. This also shows why the rule is applied to the node and not to the plates of a charging capacitor.

questions.q: Explain why connecting one more resistor in parallel always lowers the equivalent resistance while connecting one more in series always raises it, in terms of what happens to the charge carriers.
questions.concept: Series and parallel as extra path length versus extra path, related through the conductance sum
questions.why: A full answer says that a parallel resistor supplies an additional route between the same two nodes, so at the same potential difference more total current flows; since conductances add, the total conductance rises and the equivalent resistance must fall below the smallest branch. A series resistor instead lengthens the single route every carrier must take, adding another potential drop at the same current, so the resistances add and the total exceeds the largest element. A good answer also notes the check that this provides on any numerical combination.

checks.topic: Week 5 flowchart concepts treated conceptually: what each flowchart symbol means and why the notation gives it that role. Covers the process, decision, input/output, preparation, predefined process, merge, summing junction, comment and connector symbols; the rules governing how many flow lines may enter and leave each; why a flowchart needs one entry point and reachable exit points; and what breaks when those rules are ignored. Also covers why the four drawing principles are stated as principles rather than as correctness rules, and how the four flowchart types (process, workflow, swimlane, data) differ in what they are for. No hand-tracing of charts is required in this session.

questions.q: A process rectangle and a decision diamond both sit on the flow path. Why does the notation allow the diamond exactly two outgoing flow lines but the rectangle only one?
options: A process has exactly one successor - the next step - while the diamond's two exits are the mutually exclusive answers to its question, so control must be able to continue either way.
The diamond is the wider shape, so it has room for a flow line at each of its two lower vertices.
A process step might fail, and failure is shown by returning to the previous symbol rather than by drawing a second exit.
Two exits from a rectangle would mean its two successors run at the same time, which is shown with a summing junction instead.
questions.concept: Why branching is the exclusive property of the decision symbol: the number of exits encodes the number of possible continuations, not the shape's geometry.
questions.why: A rectangle states one action, after which there is one and only one next step. A diamond states a question whose yes/no answer selects between two continuations, so it needs one flow line per answer.

questions.q: Sum = 0 written before a loop and Sum = Sum + n written inside it are both assignments. Why does the notation give them different symbols?
options: Because Sum = 0 executes only once, and any step that executes only once is drawn as a hexagon.
Because the hexagon is reserved for steps that set a variable to zero or to an empty starting value.
Because an assignment outside a loop counts as input/output, while an assignment inside a loop counts as a process.
Because the preparation symbol marks a step that sets things up for the work that follows, while the process symbol marks the work itself; the distinction is the step's role, not its arithmetic.
questions.concept: The preparation symbol versus the process symbol - the deck defines preparation as the difference between steps preparing for work and steps that actually work.
questions.why: The two symbols encode a difference in purpose. Preparation sets the stage (clearing a total, setting a counter, arming a loop); process performs the computation the algorithm exists to do.

questions.q: A chart uses an on-page connector: a flow line enters a small circle labelled A, and elsewhere on the page a circle labelled A sends a flow line into Step 4. Why does the connector add nothing to the algorithm, yet a connector left without its matching partner makes the chart invalid?
options: A connector holds the value most recently computed, so an unmatched one loses that value and the steps after it read undefined data.
A connector is only a flow line drawn in two pieces, so it adds no step; unmatched, the flow line has no destination and that path can never reach a Stop symbol.
A connector counts as one step of the algorithm, so an unmatched one leaves the step count wrong and the chart cannot be turned into code.
A connector fixes the order in which the pages are read, so an unmatched one makes the page order ambiguous although the logic is still complete.
questions.concept: Connectors are pure navigation - a re-drawn flow line - and validity requires that every path still leads somewhere.
questions.why: The pair of circles is one arrow cut in half for tidiness, so it performs no operation. Cut the arrow and leave one end nowhere, and the preceding symbol has no successor, which breaks the rule that every path must be able to reach a stop.

questions.q: Why must a valid flowchart have exactly one Start terminator, while it is acceptable for it to have several Stop terminators?
options: Because the Start symbol also declares the chart's variables, and declaring them twice would be an error.
Because Stop symbols are decoration, whereas Start marks the place where the reader begins reading.
Because execution can begin in only one place, so exactly one entry point is required; but different branches may legitimately finish, so several exit points are allowed.
Because a Start symbol has no incoming flow line, so a second Start would have nothing pointing at it and could never be reached.
questions.concept: The asymmetry between entry and exit points, and what the principle 'a flowchart should have a start point and a stop point' actually constrains.
questions.why: An algorithm has a single definite beginning, so two Starts would leave it undefined which one runs. Ending is not like that: several branches may each finish the work, so each may carry its own Stop.

questions.q: Three flow lines converge. On one chart they meet at a downward-pointing triangle; on another they meet at a circle containing a cross. What is the difference in meaning?
options: The triangle joins paths that lie on a single page; the circled cross joins paths arriving from another page.
The triangle is used when the paths came from a decision; the circled cross when they came from separate Start symbols.
They mean the same thing; the circled cross is simply the older notation for a merge.
The triangle means the routes continue as one route; the circled cross means the values arriving on those routes are added together.
questions.concept: Merge versus summing junction: joining control paths is not the same operation as summing the data those paths carry.
questions.why: The merge symbol combines various paths into a single path - a statement about control flow. The summing junction shows the addition of inputs from various paths - a statement about data.

questions.q: Why is the comment or note symbol attached by a dashed line and given no flow arrows of its own?
options: Because it describes a part of the chart rather than being a step; putting it on the flow path would assert that control passes through a remark.
Because comments are added once the chart is finished, and a dashed line marks anything added afterwards.
Because a dashed line means the step is optional and may be skipped when the chart is executed.
Because comments belong to the programmer rather than to the program, and solid lines are reserved for symbols that survive into the finished code.
questions.concept: The distinction between symbols that carry control and annotations that carry none - and what a solid flow line commits you to.
questions.why: Every solid arrow says control moves from here to there. A comment is not something the machine does, so it is tied on with a dashed line, off the flow path entirely.

questions.q: One of the stated drawing principles is that flow lines should generally not cross, if possible. Why is it hedged with 'generally' and 'if possible' rather than stated flatly?
options: Because crossing flow lines silently reverse the order in which the crossed steps execute, and this must therefore be avoided in every case.
Because it is a readability rule rather than a correctness one: the arrows still mean exactly what they point at, but a crossed chart is harder to follow.
Because crossings are permitted only where a connector symbol is placed at the crossing point to disambiguate them.
Because whether lines cross depends on the drawing package used, so the principle cannot be enforced in practice.
questions.concept: Which flowchart rules are semantic (they change what the chart means) and which are presentational (they change only how easily it is read).
questions.why: Meaning lives in the arrowheads, so a crossing does not alter the algorithm. It does damage the visual clarity that is the whole reason for drawing the chart, which is why it is a strong recommendation rather than a hard rule.

questions.q: A bank wants a chart showing how a loan application moves between the customer, the branch officer and the credit department, with each party's steps kept in its own band across the page. Which of the four main flowchart types fits, and why?
options: A process flowchart, because it shows the process a product goes through along the production chain.
A data flowchart, because it shows the flow of information through the system.
A swimlane flowchart, because it allows multiple categories of activity to be shown side by side.
A workflow flowchart, because it describes the manner in which a business functions.
questions.concept: Choosing among process, workflow, swimlane and data flowcharts by what the chart must make visible - here, who owns each step.
questions.why: The requirement is parallel bands, one per actor. That is exactly the swimlane chart's defining feature; a workflow chart describes how the business functions but does not partition activity into categories.

questions.q: Explain why a decision diamond whose two exits are left unlabelled makes a flowchart untraceable, even when a reader can guess which branch was intended.
questions.concept: The labels on a decision's exits are what bind the answers of the question to particular flow lines; without them the chart carries a question but no mapping from answer to path.
questions.why: A full answer says: the diamond contributes only a question; the labels Yes/No (or True/False) are what attach each possible answer to one of the two outgoing flow lines. Without them, a tracer who evaluates the condition still cannot determine which arrow to follow, so the chart defines no behaviour for either answer - the algorithm is ambiguous, not merely untidy. It must also note that guessing from the shape of the drawing (for example assuming the downward arrow is Yes) is a reader's convention, not information the chart supplies, and different readers would trace it differently, which is exactly the ambiguity a flowchart exists to remove.

questions.q: Explain why the top-to-bottom, left-to-right direction of operation is a convention while the arrowheads on the flow lines are the actual rule.
questions.concept: Default reading direction versus explicit control flow - what actually determines the order of operations in a flowchart.
questions.why: A full answer says: the order in which a flowchart executes is defined by its flow lines and the direction of their arrowheads, symbol by symbol; the top-to-bottom, left-to-right habit only makes a chart easy to read when nothing unusual is happening, and is what lets a designer omit clutter. The moment an arrow points upwards or backwards - as every loop's back arrow does - the convention is contradicted and the arrowhead wins. It should note the consequence: you may never infer the next step from a symbol's position on the page, and a chart whose boxes sit in a neat column but whose arrows jump around means what the arrows say.

questions.q: Explain why flowcharts can be praised for simplifying and clarifying a program's logic and, in the same lecture, criticised for producing programs that are unnecessarily long and inefficient.
questions.concept: The advantages and disadvantages of flowcharts arise from the same property: the notation makes every step of control flow explicit and visible.
questions.why: A full answer says: the notation forces every step and every branch to be drawn as a separate symbol, which is precisely what makes the logic visible, checkable before coding, and communicable to other programmers and to non-technical stakeholders. The same forced explicitness means the chart offers no abstraction - no way to express a compact construct that a programming language provides in one line - so translating a chart symbol-by-symbol into code yields a longer, more roundabout program than a programmer would write directly. It should also mention the practical costs the deck lists: complex charts spilling across pages, and changes that force a redraw.

questions.q: Explain why the rectangle, the diamond and the parallelogram are between them enough to express sequence, selection and repetition - what does each construct actually demand of the notation?
questions.concept: The three control constructs reduce to two requirements the symbols already meet: a step with one successor, and a test with two.
questions.why: A full answer says: sequence needs only symbols with a single entry and a single exit, which the rectangle and parallelogram provide - stack them and control passes down the chain. Selection needs a point at which control may continue in either of two ways depending on data, which is exactly the diamond with its two labelled exits; the branches then rejoin so the chart carries on as one path. Repetition needs the same two-way test, but with one exit's flow line running backwards to a symbol already executed, so a group of symbols runs again. The essential point: nothing new is needed for looping - repetition is selection plus a backward flow line, which is why the shape alone cannot tell you which construct you are looking at.

checks.topic: Week 5 differentiation treated as problems: reading an expression and deciding which rule it needs, then executing it correctly. Covers differentiation from first principles on a simple algebraic function, the power rule with ordinary and negative or fractional indices, product and quotient rules with polynomial factors, the chain rule on a bracket raised to a power and on a root, implicit differentiation of a relation in x and y, and parametric differentiation via dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Also covers checking a finished derivative for plausibility and diagnosing exactly which step a wrong answer omitted.

questions.q: If y = (3x squared + 1) to the power 5, then dy/dx =
options: 30x(3x squared + 1) to the power 4
5(3x squared + 1) to the power 4
15x(3x squared + 1) to the power 4
6x(3x squared + 1) to the power 5
questions.concept: Chain rule on a bracket raised to a power: reduce the index, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
questions.why: With u = 3x squared + 1, dy/du = 5u to the 4 and du/dx = 6x, so dy/dx = 5(3x squared + 1)^4 times 6x = 30x(3x squared + 1)^4. Option 2 omits the inner derivative, option 3 multiplies by 3x instead of 6x, option 4 forgets to reduce the index.

questions.q: Differentiating f(x) = x squared from first principles, the quotient [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h simplifies, before the limit is taken, to
options: 2x
x + h
2x + h
2x + h squared
questions.concept: Executing the first-principles quotient: expand, subtract, cancel the single factor of h, and only then take the limit.
questions.why: (x+h)^2 - x^2 = 2xh + h^2, and dividing by h gives 2x + h. Answer 1 is the value only after the limit, and answer 4 comes from dividing h^2 by h incorrectly.

questions.q: Which route is the correct one for differentiating y = (2x + 3)/(x squared - 1)?
options: Apply the power rule to the numerator and the denominator separately and then divide the results
Use the chain rule with u = x squared - 1 and treat the numerator as a constant
Use the product rule directly on the factors (2x + 3) and (x squared - 1)
Use the quotient rule with u = 2x + 3 and v = x squared - 1
questions.concept: Recognising structure: a ratio of two functions of x calls for the quotient rule (or equivalently a product with a negative index plus the chain rule).
questions.why: The expression is a genuine quotient of two non-constant functions, so dy/dx = (u'v - uv')/v squared. Differentiating top and bottom separately is not a valid rule, and the numerator is not constant so it cannot be pulled outside a chain rule.

questions.q: If y = x cubed times (2x + 5), then dy/dx =
options: 6x squared
8x cubed + 15x squared
6x cubed + 15x squared
3x squared(2x + 5)
questions.concept: Executing the product rule and checking it against the expanded form.
questions.why: u'v + uv' = 3x^2(2x+5) + x^3(2) = 6x^3 + 15x^2 + 2x^3 = 8x^3 + 15x^2, which matches differentiating the expanded 2x^4 + 5x^3. Option 1 is the invalid u'v', option 3 drops the second term's contribution, option 4 stops after the first term.

questions.q: If y = x/(x + 1), then dy/dx =
options: -1/(x + 1) squared
1/(x + 1) squared
(2x + 1)/(x + 1) squared
questions.concept: Executing the quotient rule, including the sign of the numerator after simplification.
questions.why: [1(x+1) - x(1)]/(x+1)^2 = (x + 1 - x)/(x+1)^2 = 1/(x+1)^2. Option 1 comes from differentiating top and bottom separately, option 2 from reversing the numerator order, option 4 from adding rather than subtracting.

questions.q: A student writes dy/dx = 4(x squared + 3) cubed for y = (x squared + 3) to the power 4. Which single step was omitted?
options: Multiplying by the derivative of the inner function, 2x
Reducing the outer index from 4 to 2 rather than to 3
Expanding the bracket first, which is required for powers above 3
Adding a separate term for the derivative of the constant 3
questions.concept: Diagnosing a chain-rule omission: the power rule alone is only valid when the base is x itself.
questions.why: The outer power was handled correctly but the inner function was not differentiated, so the answer should be 8x(x squared + 3) cubed. Reducing the index by one is correct, expansion is never obligatory, and the constant inside contributes nothing extra.

questions.q: For the circle x squared + y squared = 25, dy/dx =
options: -y/x
-x/y
x/y
-2x/y
questions.concept: Implicit differentiation: apply d/dx to both sides, carry the dy/dx factor on the y term, then make dy/dx the subject.
questions.why: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0 gives dy/dx = -2x/2y = -x/y. Option 1 inverts the variables, option 3 loses the sign from moving 2x across, option 4 cancels the 2 in only one place.

questions.q: Having obtained dy/dx = 1/(x + 1) squared for y = x/(x + 1), which observation is a genuine check that the answer is plausible?
options: The numerator of the derivative has the same degree as the numerator of the original function
Both the function and its derivative are undefined at x = 0
Substituting x = -1 gives a finite value in both the function and the derivative
The derivative is positive wherever it is defined, matching a function that increases on each branch
questions.concept: Checking a derivative against the behaviour of the original function: sign of the derivative versus increasing or decreasing behaviour, and matching points of failure.
questions.why: Writing y = 1 - 1/(x+1) shows the function rises on each side of x = -1, and 1/(x+1)^2 is indeed positive everywhere it exists, so the sign agrees. The other statements are simply false: both expressions are perfectly well defined at x = 0 and both break down at x = -1, and degree of the numerator carries no such guarantee.

questions.q: Explain why differentiating y = (2x + 1) cubed by the chain rule and by first expanding the bracket must give the same answer, and explain where the factor 2 in the chain-rule result shows up in the expanded calculation.
questions.concept: The chain rule as a shortcut that must agree with direct expansion; locating the inner derivative inside the expanded coefficients.
questions.why: A full answer notes that both routes differentiate the same function, so agreement is forced. Chain rule: 3(2x+1)^2 times 2 = 6(2x+1)^2 = 24x^2 + 24x + 6. Expansion: (2x+1)^3 = 8x^3 + 12x^2 + 6x + 1, whose derivative is 24x^2 + 24x + 6. The factor 2 shows up in the expansion as the powers of 2 carried by the binomial coefficients: every term picked up a factor of 2 for each x it contains, which is exactly the rate at which the inner function 2x+1 responds to x. The general point is that the chain rule packages that inner sensitivity into a single multiplier instead of spreading it through every coefficient.

questions.q: Explain why, for x = t squared and y = t cubed, dy/dt on its own is not the gradient of the curve, and explain why dividing by dx/dt repairs this.
questions.concept: Parametric differentiation: separating the rate of tracing from the geometry of the curve.
questions.why: A full answer says dy/dt = 3t^2 measures how fast y changes with the parameter, which depends on how the curve is traced rather than on its shape; re-parametrising (for instance t replaced by 2t) changes dy/dt but cannot change the gradient of the same curve. Since dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt) by the chain rule, dividing by dx/dt = 2t removes the tracing speed and leaves the purely geometric ratio dy/dx = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2, valid for t not zero. It should add that at t = 0 both derivatives vanish and the formula gives no gradient, which corresponds to the cusp of this curve at the origin.

questions.q: Explain why d/dx(1/x squared) can be obtained either by the quotient rule or by the power rule with a negative index, and explain why the two must agree.
questions.concept: Equivalent routes to the same derivative, and rewriting as a negative power as the cheaper route.
questions.why: A full answer performs both. Power rule: 1/x^2 = x^-2, so the derivative is -2x^-3 = -2/x^3. Quotient rule with u = 1, v = x^2: (0 times x^2 - 1 times 2x)/x^4 = -2x/x^4 = -2/x^3. They must agree because 1/x^2 and x^-2 are the same function, and a function has only one derivative at each point; the rules are theorems about that single object, not competing definitions. It should also observe that the quotient rule is the more laborious route here because the numerator is constant, and that the rules themselves are linked, since the quotient rule follows from the product rule applied to u times v^-1.

questions.q: Explain why a student who differentiates x squared times y = 6 as 2xy = 0 has gone wrong, and state what the correct working gives.
questions.concept: Diagnosing a failed implicit differentiation: the left side is a product of two functions of x, so both the product rule and the chain-rule factor dy/dx are required.
questions.why: A full answer identifies two errors. First, x^2 times y is a product of two x-dependent quantities, so the product rule is needed rather than differentiating x^2 and copying y across. Second, y is a function of x, so differentiating it with respect to x yields dy/dx, not zero and not nothing. Correct working: d/dx(x^2 y) = 2xy + x^2 (dy/dx), and the right-hand side gives 0 since 6 is constant, so 2xy + x^2 dy/dx = 0 and dy/dx = -2y/x (x not zero). A good answer may confirm it by solving explicitly: y = 6x^-2 gives dy/dx = -12x^-3, and -2y/x = -12x^-2/x = -12x^-3, which matches.

checks.topic: Problem hour on Week 5 circuit analysis. Reducing a network by the series and parallel rules and recognising when that reduction is illegal. Setting up Kirchhoff equations for a two-loop network of two batteries with internal resistance and one shared resistor: choosing branch-current arrows, writing the junction equation, writing each loop equation with correct signs for the emf and IR terms, and solving for all three currents. Reading a negative current in the solution, computing terminal potential difference and power, and checking a finished answer independently. Includes diagnosing a wrong route and finding the balance condition of a bridge.

questions.q: A 30 V battery of internal resistance 1.0 ohm feeds a 5.0 ohm resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 ohm and 12.0 ohm. What current does the battery deliver?
questions.concept: Reducing a mixed network in the right order, and remembering that internal resistance is part of the total
questions.why: The parallel pair gives 4.0 ohm, so the total is 1.0 plus 5.0 plus 4.0 equals 10.0 ohm and I equals 30 divided by 10.0 equals 3.0 A.

questions.q: For that same circuit another student writes R total equals 1.0 plus 5.0 plus 6.0 plus 12.0 equals 24 ohm. Which specific mistake is that?
options: They included the internal resistance, which should have been left out of the total resistance.
They used resistance values where the calculation requires conductances to be summed instead.
They forgot that the 5.0 ohm resistor carries a smaller current than the battery itself delivers.
They added the 6.0 ohm and 12.0 ohm as if in series, although both lie across the same pair of nodes.
questions.concept: The test for series (same current) versus parallel (same pair of nodes), applied before any arithmetic
questions.why: Two elements connected between the same two nodes are in parallel and must be combined by the reciprocal rule; adding them treats them as if the same current passed through both, which it does not.

questions.q: Between nodes a and b are three branches: a 12 V battery with r equals 1 ohm, a 6 V battery with r equals 1 ohm (both with their positive terminals towards a), and a 4 ohm resistor. Take I1 and I2 as flowing b to a inside the batteries and I3 as flowing a to b through the resistor. Walking b to a through the 12 V battery and then a to b through the resistor, the loop equation is
options: 12 minus (1)I1 minus 4 I3 equals 0
12 plus (1)I1 minus 4 I3 equals 0
12 minus (1)I1 plus 4 I3 equals 0
minus 12 minus (1)I1 minus 4 I3 equals 0
questions.concept: Applying the four traversal sign rules to build a loop equation containing an emf, an internal resistance and an external resistor
questions.why: Entering the battery at its minus terminal gives plus 12; the internal resistance is traversed with I1, giving minus I1 r; the 4 ohm resistor is traversed with I3, giving minus 4 I3.

questions.q: Solving that network with the junction equation I3 equals I1 plus I2 and the two loop equations gives which value for the current in the 6 V branch?
options: plus 2.0 A
plus 1.2 A
minus 2.0 A
minus 4.0 A
questions.concept: Executing the elimination on a two-loop system and keeping the signs through the substitution
questions.why: I1 equals 12 minus 4 I3 and I2 equals 6 minus 4 I3; substituting into I3 equals I1 plus I2 gives 9 I3 equals 18, so I3 equals 2.0 A and I2 equals 6 minus 8 equals minus 2.0 A.

questions.q: What does that negative value tell you physically about the 6 V battery in that circuit?
options: Its effective emf has fallen below 6 V once the internal resistance is taken into account.
It has been short-circuited by the stronger battery and is carrying no useful current at all.
It delivers 2.0 A to the circuit, the minus sign being only an artefact of the bookkeeping.
Charge enters its positive terminal, so it is being charged and is absorbing 12 W from the circuit.
questions.concept: Translating the sign of a solved current back into physical behaviour of a source
questions.why: The true current is 2.0 A opposite to the assumed arrow, so it flows into the positive terminal; the 6 V source therefore absorbs energy at a rate epsilon times I equals 6 times 2.0 equals 12 W.

questions.q: With I1 equals 4.0 A, I2 equals minus 2.0 A and I3 equals 2.0 A, what is the potential difference V ab across the three parallel branches?
questions.concept: Computing a node potential difference along any branch, including a branch whose current came out negative
questions.why: Along the 4 ohm branch V ab equals I3 R equals 2.0 times 4 equals 8.0 V, and the same value follows as 12 minus 4.0 times 1 along branch one and as 6 minus (minus 2.0) times 1 along branch two.

questions.q: Which computation is a genuinely independent check on that solution rather than a restatement of it?
options: Re-substituting the three currents into the two loop equations that were used to solve the network.
Comparing the total power delivered by the sources with the power dissipated and absorbed elsewhere.
Confirming that every current in the final answer has come out as a positive number.
Confirming that the sum of the three branch resistances equals the network's equivalent resistance.
questions.concept: What counts as an independent check: a relation not used in deriving the answer
questions.why: The power balance uses squares of the currents and is not one of the equations solved, so it can fail where re-substitution cannot; here 48 W delivered equals 36 W dissipated plus 12 W absorbed.

questions.q: A bridge has R1 equals 100 ohm above R2 equals 200 ohm in one branch and R3 equals 300 ohm above an unknown R4 in the other, with a galvanometer joining the two midpoints. What value of R4 gives zero galvanometer current?
options: 150 ohm
400 ohm
600 ohm
200 ohm
questions.concept: The balance condition R1 over R2 equals R3 over R4, and why balance makes the network reducible again
questions.why: Zero galvanometer current means both midpoints are at the same potential, so both branches divide the same p.d. in the same ratio: 100 over 200 equals 300 over R4 gives R4 equals 600 ohm.

questions.q: Explain why drawing a branch-current arrow in the wrong direction cannot make a Kirchhoff solution wrong, and state exactly where in the algebra the mistaken guess shows up.
questions.concept: Current arrows as sign definitions; linearity of the junction and loop equations
questions.why: A full answer says the arrow defines which direction counts as positive current in that branch rather than claiming anything about the circuit; every junction and loop equation is then written consistently with that definition. Because both rules are linear in the currents, replacing a current by its negative reproduces the same system, so the solution is unchanged in magnitude. The mistaken guess appears solely as a minus sign on that current in the answer, which is read as the same current flowing the other way; nothing needs recalculating.

questions.q: Explain why, for the two-battery network above, writing a third loop equation (around the loop containing both batteries) adds nothing to the two already written.
questions.concept: Independence of equations: a third loop is a linear combination of the other two, and the count of equations must match the count of unknowns
questions.why: A full answer says there are three unknown branch currents, so exactly three independent equations are needed and one junction plus two loops supplies them. The loop through both batteries is traced by following loop one forwards and loop two backwards, so its equation is the difference of the two already written and is satisfied automatically by any solution of them. Adding it produces a dependent system, not extra information, and a good answer notes the general rule that only branches not yet used create new independent loops.

questions.q: Explain why a power balance is a stronger check on a finished Kirchhoff solution than substituting the currents back into the equations that were used to obtain them.
questions.concept: Independent versus circular verification, and the extra information carried by the quadratic power relation
questions.why: A full answer says that re-substitution can only detect arithmetic slips made after those equations were written; if an equation itself carries a wrong sign, the wrong solution satisfies it perfectly, so the check passes on a wrong answer. The power balance is a separate physical statement, quadratic in the currents rather than linear, and was not used in deriving the solution, so a sign error in an emf or IR term generally breaks it. A good answer adds that sources with a negative current must be entered as absorbing power for the balance to close.

questions.q: Explain why the potential difference between the two nodes of that network must come out the same whichever of the three branches you compute it along, and what it means if two routes disagree.
questions.concept: Single-valuedness of potential as the content of the loop rule, used as a diagnostic
questions.why: A full answer says the two nodes have definite potentials, so their difference is one number and any branch joining them must reproduce it; the statement that two routes agree is exactly the loop rule for the loop those two branches form. A disagreement therefore means one of the loop equations has not in fact been satisfied, which locates the error to the branch whose route disagrees, usually a wrong emf sign, an omitted Ir term, or a current sign not carried through. A good answer shows the three routes for this circuit giving 8.0 V.

checks.topic: Week 5 flowchart concepts treated as practice. Every chart is described in words and must be traced by hand: the sum-of-five-numbers loop from the lecture, a compare-two-numbers selection, and a fault-finding lamp chart. The session asks what a described chart prints for given inputs, which construct a fragment implements, how to lay out the opening steps of a chart for a stated problem, and how to diagnose a chart that loops forever, resets an accumulator, reads one item too many, or leaves a path with no route to Stop. It does not ask for symbol definitions in the abstract.

questions.q: Trace this chart. Start; Sum = 0; Count = 0; then at point A, Enter n; Sum = Sum + n; Count = Count + 1; then a decision 'Is Count < 5?' whose Yes exit runs back to A and whose No exit runs to Print Sum; Stop. The numbers waiting to be entered are, in order, 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9. What is printed?
options: Nothing - the chart never reaches Print Sum
questions.concept: Hand-tracing a counted loop: how many passes the test Count < 5 permits, and which numbers are therefore consumed.
questions.why: The loop runs while Count is still below 5, so it makes five passes and consumes 3, 1, 4, 1 and 5. On the fifth pass Count becomes 5, the test fails, and the accumulated 14 is printed; the 9 is never read.

questions.q: Trace this chart. Start; Total = 0; K = 0; then at point A, Enter x; Total = Total + x; then a decision 'Is K < 3?' whose Yes exit runs back to A and whose No exit runs to K = K + 1, then Print Total, then Stop. What happens when the chart is executed?
options: It reads three numbers and prints their total.
It reads four numbers and prints their total, one number too many.
It stops at once without reading any number, because K is still 0.
It reads numbers forever, because K is only changed on the branch that is never taken.
questions.concept: Diagnosing a non-terminating loop: the control variable must be updated on the path that is actually repeated.
questions.why: K is 0 when the decision is first reached, so the Yes exit is taken and control returns to A. Nothing on that circuit alters K, so the test yields the same answer on every pass and the K = K + 1 box on the No exit is never executed.

questions.q: Trace this chart. Start; Read A and B; a decision 'Is A > B?' whose Yes exit leads to Print A and whose No exit leads to Print B; both then meet and go to Stop. The values entered are A = 7 and B = 7. Which path is taken, and what is printed?
options: The No path is taken, and B is printed - the value 7.
The Yes path is taken, and A is printed - the value 7.
Neither path is taken; the chart cannot resolve A equal to B and halts at the diamond.
Both paths are taken, so 7 is printed twice.
questions.concept: Evaluating a strict comparison at the boundary: 'greater than' is false when the two values are equal, so equality falls to the No branch.
questions.why: 7 > 7 is false, so the decision answers No and control follows that single exit to Print B. The printed number happens to be the same either way, which is exactly why the path, not the value, is what must be traced.

questions.q: Take this chart. Start; Count = 0; Sum = 0; then at point A, Enter n; Sum = Sum + n; Count = Count + 1; decision 'Is Count < 5?' Yes exit back to A, No exit to Print Sum; Stop. Now the back arrow is redrawn so that it lands on the box Sum = 0 instead of on A. The numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 are entered. What is printed?
options: 30 - the same as before, since the numbers entered have not changed.
Nothing; the chart now loops forever and never reaches Print Sum.
10, the last number entered.
0, because Sum is cleared immediately before it is printed.
questions.concept: Where a loop's back arrow lands decides which boxes are inside the loop - here it drags the accumulator's initialisation inside, destroying the running total.
questions.why: Count = 0 stays outside the loop, so the counter still climbs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the chart exits after five passes. Sum = 0 is now inside, so it is cleared at the top of every pass and holds only the number read on the final pass.

questions.q: You must lay out a flowchart that reads ten numbers, which may be positive or negative, and prints the largest of them. Which opening is correct?
options: Set Max = 0 first, then read each of the ten numbers in turn and replace Max whenever the number read is larger.
Read the first number into Max, then read the remaining nine and replace Max whenever a larger number arrives.
Read all ten numbers first, then set Max to the last number read and print it.
Set Max = 0 and Count = 10, decrease Count by one on every pass, and print Max once Count reaches 0.
questions.concept: Converting a stated problem into flowchart steps: an extreme-value accumulator must be seeded with a member of the data, not with an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: Seeding Max with the first actual number guarantees it starts at a value the data really contains, so the comparisons can only move it upward to the true maximum. Any fixed seed such as 0 is simply a value that may be larger than every number in the list.

questions.q: A student hands in this chart. Start; Read mark; a decision 'Is mark 50 or more?' whose Yes exit leads to Print 'Pass' and then to Stop. The No exit is drawn leaving the diamond but its flow line ends in empty space. What exactly is wrong with the chart?
options: Nothing is wrong; a branch on which there is nothing to do may be left blank.
The diamond should have been a rectangle, since only one action follows it.
One path can never reach a Stop symbol, so for a mark below 50 the chart specifies no behaviour at all.
The chart is invalid because the box Print 'Pass' has two flow lines entering it.
questions.concept: Validity checking: every path leaving a decision must eventually reach a Stop, so a dangling branch is an undefined case rather than an empty one.
questions.why: Tracing a mark of 40 leads out of the diamond and then nowhere, so the algorithm has no defined behaviour for that input. The fix is to run the No branch to a Stop, directly or after whatever it should do first.

questions.q: Trace this fault-finding chart. Start 'Lamp does not work'; decision 'Lamp plugged in?' whose No exit leads to Plug in lamp and then Stop, and whose Yes exit leads to the decision 'Bulb burned out?'; that second decision's Yes exit leads to Replace bulb and then Stop, and its No exit leads to Repair lamp and then Stop. The lamp is plugged in and its bulb is sound. Which action boxes are executed?
options: Plug in lamp, and then Repair lamp.
Replace bulb, and nothing else.
Plug in lamp, and nothing else.
Repair lamp, and nothing else.
questions.concept: Tracing a chain of selections: each decision's answer picks one exit, so exactly one action box on the chain is reached.
questions.why: Plugged in gives Yes at the first diamond, which skips Plug in lamp entirely; a sound bulb gives No at the second, which skips Replace bulb. Only Repair lamp lies on the traced path.

questions.q: In the chart Start; Sum = 0; Count = 0; A: Enter n; Sum = Sum + n; Count = Count + 1; decision 'Is Count < 5?' Yes back to A, No to Print Sum; Stop - the test alone is changed to 'Is Count less than or equal to 5?'. Everything else is unchanged. What is the effect?
options: Six numbers are read instead of five.
Four numbers are read instead of five.
Five numbers are still read, because the two tests agree at the boundary value.
The chart loops forever, since Count can never exceed 5.
questions.concept: Off-by-one at a loop's exit condition: the exit test is evaluated after the counter has been incremented, so relaxing it by one grants one extra pass.
questions.why: After the fifth pass Count is 5; the old test 5 < 5 fails and the loop ends, but 5 is less than or equal to 5 is true, so a sixth pass runs and Count reaches 6, at which point the loop ends.

questions.q: Explain why a loop whose control variable is updated only on the branch that is not taken runs forever, in terms of what the decision symbol re-evaluates on each pass.
questions.concept: Loop termination requires that some step on the repeated circuit changes a value the exit test depends on.
questions.why: A full answer says: the diamond does not remember anything between passes - it re-evaluates its condition from the current values of the variables every time control reaches it. Termination therefore depends entirely on some box on the repeated circuit changing a variable the condition reads. If the increment sits on the exit branch, it lies outside the circuit that repeats, so every pass presents the diamond with the identical data and it must return the identical answer, sending control round again. The answer should note the fix - the update must be placed between the loop's entry point and the diamond - and that this is a property of the arrows, not of the arithmetic in the box.

questions.q: Explain why a largest-number chart that begins Max = 0 prints the wrong answer when every number read is negative, and why seeding Max with the first number read repairs it.
questions.concept: An accumulator that must end up holding one of the data values has to be seeded from the data, not from a constant that may lie outside their range.
questions.why: A full answer says: the loop only ever replaces Max when a number read is larger than it, so Max can move upward but never downward from its seed. With Max = 0 and, say, the numbers -3, -9 and -12, no comparison ever succeeds, and the chart prints 0 - a value that was never in the list at all. Seeding Max with the first number read means Max already holds a genuine member of the data and is a legitimate answer if nothing beats it, so the remaining comparisons can only improve it. The answer should also note that the loop must then run over the remaining nine numbers, not all ten, or the counter is wrong by one.

questions.q: Explain why the point at which a loop's back arrow lands - and not the contents of the boxes - decides whether a running total survives from one pass to the next.
questions.concept: The back arrow's landing point defines the loop body: any initialisation caught inside it is re-executed every pass.
questions.why: A full answer says: the flow lines, not the layout, define which symbols form the repeated circuit; everything between the arrow's landing point and the decision is executed again on every pass, and everything above the landing point runs once. Sum = Sum + n is unchanged in either version, so the boxes are not what differ. If the back arrow lands below Sum = 0, the accumulator keeps its total and the chart sums the whole series; if it lands on or above Sum = 0, the accumulator is cleared at the top of every pass and can only ever report the last item. It should note the same reasoning applied to the counter: dragging Count = 0 inside the loop resets the counter too and the loop never ends.

questions.q: Explain why hand-tracing a chart with a table of variable values catches an off-by-one that simply reading the chart does not.
questions.concept: Boundary behaviour depends on the order of increment and test within a pass, which is visible in a trace of successive values but invisible in the wording of the condition.
questions.why: A full answer says: reading 'Is Count < 5?' invites you to translate the condition into an intention - five numbers - but whether five actually happens depends on where the counter starts, where it is incremented relative to the test, and whether the test is strict. A table with one row per pass, recording the value of every variable at the moment the diamond is reached, makes the boundary pass explicit: you can see that Count is already 5 when the test is applied for the fifth time, and that the fifth number was consumed before the test ran. It should note that the decisive rows are the first and the last, and that off-by-one errors are exactly the errors that look correct when read and only show up when counted.

recapCandidates.topic: The arrows you draw for the branch currents are not a guess you have to get right; they are a definition of which direction counts as positive in each branch. The signs in a loop equation are then fixed by the direction you walk the loop, not by the direction the current really flows. A current that comes out negative is a correct answer with the arrow drawn the other way round.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students believe the arrows are a prediction that must be correct before the equations are valid, so a negative current reads to them as an error to be hunted down; the belief survives because in every single-loop circuit with one battery the obvious guess really is the true direction, so guessing right and being right never come apart until a second emf is introduced.
whyQuestions: Why are we allowed to draw a current arrow before we know which way the current actually flows?
Why does the sign of an IR term depend on the direction you walk the loop, while the sign of an emf term does not?
Why does reversing one arrow change nothing except the sign of that one current in the answer?
Why does a negative current in the answer not mean an equation was written wrongly, and what test separates the two cases?
Why can you draw all three branch arrows pointing into the same node and still get the right answer out?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says the arrow defines what counts as positive current in that branch, and that every junction and loop equation is then written consistently with that definition, so the physics enters only through the emfs, the resistances and the way the circuit is wired.
It says both Kirchhoff rules are linear in the currents, so replacing a current by its negative reproduces the same system; a reversed definition therefore returns the same magnitude with the opposite sign, and the answer is read off, not redone.
It gives the discriminating test between a reversed arrow and a real mistake: put the solution back into the junction equation and every loop equation, and check the power balance; if they all close, the minus sign is physical and means the current runs against the arrow.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Nodes a (top) and b (bottom) are joined by three parallel branches: a 12 V battery with internal resistance 1 ohm, a 6 V battery with internal resistance 1 ohm (both positive terminals towards a), and a 4 ohm resistor. Assume I1 and I2 flow b to a inside the batteries and I3 flows a to b through the resistor. Junction rule at a: I3 = I1 + I2. Loop with the 12 V battery and the resistor, walked b to a then a to b: enter the battery at minus and leave at plus for +12, traverse r1 with the current for -(1)I1, traverse the 4 ohm with I3 for -4I3, giving 12 - I1 - 4I3 = 0. The same walk on the second branch gives 6 - I2 - 4I3 = 0. Hence I1 = 12 - 4I3 and I2 = 6 - 4I3; substituting into the junction equation, I3 = 18 - 8I3, so 9I3 = 18 and I3 = 2.0 A. Then I1 = 4.0 A and I2 = 6 - 8 = -2.0 A. The minus sign is the whole point: the 6 V branch really carries 2.0 A from a to b, into its own positive terminal, so that battery is being charged. Check the answer three ways: the junction gives 4.0 + (-2.0) = 2.0 A; V_ab is 12 - 4.0(1) = 8.0 V along branch one, 6 - (-2.0)(1) = 8.0 V along branch two and 2.0 x 4 = 8.0 V along the resistor; and the power balance gives 12 x 4.0 = 48 W delivered against 16 + 4 + 16 = 36 W dissipated plus 6 x 2.0 = 12 W absorbed by the charging battery, which is 48 W.

recapCandidates.topic: On a flowchart, a loop is not a symbol - it is a decision diamond plus a flow line that runs backwards. Which boxes get repeated is decided entirely by where that backward arrow lands, so moving the arrow by one box changes the algorithm even though every box still says exactly what it said before.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students read a flowchart the way they read a page, top to bottom, and treat the boxes as the meaning and the arrows as joining-up; this works perfectly for pure sequence and for selection, where the arrows do run downward, so it survives every chart until the first one with a back arrow.
whyQuestions: Why does the diamond need two exits when a rectangle needs only one?
Why can the same diamond mean selection in one chart and repetition in another - what in the drawing tells them apart?
Why does a loop whose counter is incremented on the exit branch run forever, when the increment box is plainly there on the page?
Why does moving the back arrow from below Sum = 0 to above it change what the chart prints, when not one box has been edited?
Why can you not tell how many times a loop runs by reading its condition, and what must you do instead?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Names the mechanism: the flow lines, not the vertical layout, define the repeated circuit - every symbol between the back arrow's landing point and the diamond runs again on each pass, everything above it runs once.
Shows the consequence in both directions: initialisation caught inside the circuit is undone every pass (the accumulator loses its total, or the counter resets and the loop never ends), and an update stranded outside the circuit never executes, so the diamond re-evaluates identical data and answers identically forever.
Gives the test to apply to any chart: find the backward arrow, mark the symbols it encloses, then trace a table of variable values pass by pass rather than reading the condition and trusting what it sounds like.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Draw the lecture's chart at the board: Start; Count = 0; Sum = 0; then label the next box A: Enter n; Sum = Sum + n; Count = Count + 1; then the diamond 'Is Count < 5?' with Yes running back to A and No running to Print Sum; Stop. Trace it with 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 in a three-column table (n, Sum, Count): pass 1 gives 2, 2, 1; pass 2 gives 4, 6, 2; pass 3 gives 6, 12, 3; pass 4 gives 8, 20, 4; pass 5 gives 10, 30, 5, at which point 5 < 5 is false and 30 is printed. Now change nothing except the back arrow, so that it lands on Sum = 0 instead of on A, and re-trace: Count is still outside the loop and still climbs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the chart still exits after five passes, but Sum is cleared at the top of every pass, giving 2, then 4, then 6, then 8, then 10, and the chart prints 10. Finally move the arrow up one box further, onto Count = 0: now the counter resets too, the diamond is handed Count = 1 on every pass, 1 < 5 is true forever and the chart never reaches Print Sum. Three algorithms, identical boxes, one arrow moved twice.
